key_findings.note: Finding as stated. In the note, the regular-use bar of Figure 6 measures about 23% at 300 dpi (card: 24%), within reading error.

key_findings.correction: Among veteran addicts (men addicted in Vietnam) who returned to narcotics, the variables in Table 2 failed to predict re-addiction: behaviour problems before service; parents' substance abuse, arrest or psychiatric care; substance use in Vietnam (types, duration, injection); IQ; draftee or volunteer; combat; military discipline problems; demographic characteristics. The text says the social and behavioural variables that had explained who became addicted in Vietnam and which ex-addicts used again after return were of no use in explaining which relapsers became re-addicted. The author suggests vulnerability to re-addiction may be biological, saying it is not known whether it is present from birth or created by the drug, and that different factors operate at each transition (to use, to addiction, to remission, to relapse).
key_findings.note: The card says 'veterans' (Table 2: veteran addicts), 'parents' substance use' (Table 2: substance abuse), and that the listed variables had predicted use in Vietnam; combat, for one, had not (p. 1049).

key_findings.correction: Other studies cited as consistent: 50 untreated people free of heroin addiction for at least 2 years had a median addiction of 5.7 years (Waldorf & Biernacki, 1979); among young men 18-28 registered with Selective Service, 13% of those reporting heroin use had been treated, and 27% of the untreated against 65% of the treated had used heroin in the past year (O'Donnell et al., 1976); 25% of Harlem youths aged 18-23 who had used heroin twice or more had used it in the current year, 16% of the untreated (Brunswick, 1979); in the ECA, substance abuse had the shortest mean duration of any psychiatric disorder, 2.7 years (estimated from ages at first and last problem), and only one in five people dependent on or abusing an illicit drug had had any treatment; most of these cases were not heroin addicts (marijuana was the most common drug of abuse).
key_findings.note: The source says most ECA cases were not heroin addicts; the card's 'most of them not for heroin' reads as most of the treated being treated for other drugs.

risk_of_bias.note: Design narrative-review (a lecture reviewing the author's own cohort), instrument none-applicable with the editors' checklist, overall high (worst domains: no search, reliance on own studies): all agreed.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible: the data-based statements stay within the data and opinions are marked as hers. The weakest step, the 'not unique' answer resting on indirect civilian studies, is already set out in 'claimed'.

missed: sample.recruitment: 13,280 was the researchers' own estimate of September returnees; the Department of Defense's later revised estimate, from the planes' lading documents, came within 3% of it (p. 1043). The card says the true number was later estimated at 13,280.

Context for the treatment findings: the only rise in VA cases came from a DoD rule delaying discharge by 30 days, spent by drug-positive soldiers in a VA drug programme; they arrived already detoxified and in no obvious need of treatment (p. 1048).

Item (6), Zinberg and Jacobson's 'chippers' (recreational heroin users who never became addicted), is cited (p. 1050) but appears nowhere on the card; the gap text counts six supporting studies where design_detail counts seven.
The first interviews were all completed within 6 months, after a funding delay of 8 months (pp. 1042-1043): the source of the 8-12-month window in reporting issue 2.
